name: decompose
reasoning: Decomposed into 66 verifiable statement(s). Completeness check passed. Grouped into 8 reasoning segment(s).

statements: The key question is not the initial wide-complex tachycardia.
The initial wide-complex tachycardia is already well characterized as left posterior fascicular idiopathic left ventricular tachycardia (ILVT).
The key question is the mechanism of the new narrow-complex tachycardia.
The new narrow-complex tachycardia appeared abruptly during radiofrequency ablation.
Salient findings for the original arrhythmia strongly support fascicular VT.
The heart is structurally normal.
The patient had recurrent palpitations.
The original arrhythmia was a wide-complex tachycardia with right bundle branch block morphology and left-axis deviation.
The original arrhythmia was reproducibly inducible with RV burst pacing and isoprenaline.
The original arrhythmia was sensitive to verapamil.
The original arrhythmia had a negative HV interval.
Atrial dissociation from ventricular activity was present during rapid atrial pacing.
Progressive fusion during atrial overdrive pacing is consistent with ventricular tachycardia.
Mapping showed presystolic Purkinje potentials in the left posterior septum.
Ablation was delivered in the left posterior septum.
The narrow-complex tachycardia emerged immediately during RF delivery at the fascicular VT site.
The narrow-complex tachycardia had a regular narrow QRS of 85 ms.
The narrow-complex tachycardia had a cycle length of 281 ms.
The narrow-complex tachycardia had 1:1 ventriculoatrial conduction.
The narrow-complex tachycardia had a relatively short VA interval.
The narrow-complex tachycardia had concentric atrial activation.
These findings point toward a supraventricular tachycardia using the AV node/His region rather than ongoing ventricular tachycardia.
A narrow QRS with short VA and concentric atrial activation is most typical of AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT).
A narrow QRS with short VA and concentric atrial activation is less commonly typical of orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia using a septal accessory pathway.
A narrow QRS with short VA and concentric atrial activation is less commonly typical of atrial tachycardia.
Baseline EP study showed no manifest preexcitation.
Baseline EP study showed no concealed accessory pathway conduction.
The absence of manifest preexcitation argues against orthodromic AVRT.
The absence of concealed accessory pathway conduction argues against orthodromic AVRT.
Earliest atrial activation in the narrow tachycardia is described as concentric rather than eccentric.
Concentric atrial activation argues against most accessory pathways.
Atrial tachycardia is less likely because the VA interval was relatively short.
Atrial tachycardia is less likely because the pattern arose abruptly during ablation in a setting where AV nodal reentry can be triggered by catheter/thermal effects.
The baseline study reportedly showed no dual AV nodal physiology.
Absence of demonstrable dual AV nodal physiology does not exclude AVNRT.
The ablation location was the mid-apical posterior interventricular septum.
The ablation location was near the left posterior fascicle/Purkinje network.
During ablation of ILVT, interruption of the ventricular reentry circuit can terminate the VT.
The resulting retrograde conduction to the atrium may permit initiation of a coincident supraventricular reentry.
The narrow-complex rhythm is best explained not as a transformed fascicular VT.
The narrow-complex rhythm is best explained as a separate supraventricular tachycardia unmasked or induced during RF delivery.
Typical slow-fast AVNRT fits best because of the narrow QRS.
Typical slow-fast AVNRT fits best because of the short VA interval.
Typical slow-fast AVNRT fits best because of concentric atrial activation.
Typical slow-fast AVNRT fits best because of the lack of evidence for an accessory pathway.
Orthodromic AVRT is less likely because there was no evidence of manifest accessory pathway conduction at baseline.
Orthodromic AVRT is less likely because there was no evidence of concealed accessory pathway conduction at baseline.
Orthodromic AVRT is less likely because the atrial activation was concentric.
Atrial tachycardia is less likely because short VA/concentric activation favors AV nodal reentry over a focal atrial source.
Junctional tachycardia could produce a narrow complex with short VA, especially during ablation.
The description of a sustained regular tachycardia with 1:1 VA conduction after abrupt transition is more in keeping with AVNRT than transient accelerated junctional rhythm.
The most likely mechanism is AV nodal reentry.
The most likely mechanism is specifically typical slow-fast AVNRT.
Typical slow-fast AVNRT was induced coincidentally during RF ablation of the fascicular VT.
Abrupt onset of regular narrow-complex tachycardia during RF delivery supports typical AVNRT.
Short VA interval supports typical AVNRT.
1:1 VA conduction supports typical AVNRT.
Concentric atrial activation supports typical AVNRT.
There was no evidence of accessory pathway conduction.
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia via a concealed septal accessory pathway can cause narrow-complex tachycardia with 1:1 VA conduction.
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia via a concealed septal accessory pathway is less likely in this case.
Focal atrial tachycardia could present as narrow-complex tachycardia.
Focal atrial tachycardia is less likely in this case.
Thermal injury during ablation can provoke junctional rhythms.
The sustained regular tachycardia pattern with 1:1 VA conduction is more characteristic of AVNRT than junctional tachycardia.
The final diagnosis is typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (slow-fast AVNRT).
